reading.body:
Six interactive estimators cover the questions that decide whether an AI project is viable: token cost, GPU memory, context window fit, training cost, energy and carbon, and return on investment.

The set is organized around arithmetic rather than opinion. Each estimator shows its own calculation and states what it excludes, which makes the assumptions inspectable instead of hidden. For AI work specifically, these are the quantities that turn a proposal into a budget: how much memory a model needs, how much context it can hold, what training and inference cost, and what energy that consumption implies.

The energy and carbon estimator is the one that connects to the physical constraint. Compute is downstream of buildings and power, so a tool that estimates energy use is estimating demand on the grid, not just a line item. The return on investment estimator closes the loop by asking whether the resulting cost is justified.

What this data does not contain is any actual numbers, results, or worked examples. It names six estimators and their subjects, and nothing about their inputs, accuracy, or the range of cases they handle. A reader should treat this as an index of the questions worth asking, not as evidence about any particular answer.
